shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Seventy-one percent. {p} In 1995, the average Slovenian was seventy-one percent richer than the average Pole, on income adjusted for prices. {pp} This year, in the IMF's numbers, the gap is under four percent. {p} And by 2031, in the IMF's forecast, it's about half a percent.

Slovenia was the richest part of the old Yugoslavia. {p} When it joined the European Union in 2004, it was richer than Czechia, Hungary and Poland. {pp} In 2007, it was the first of the new members to adopt the euro. {p} <soft>So how did a country this far ahead end up almost tied?</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series about who's passing whom in Europe, and Poland keeps showing up. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one. {p} Now, the head start.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Slovenia's GDP per capita (PPP) as % of Poland's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Slovenia as a share of Poland, adjusted for prices. {p} In 1992, a hundred and seventy-six percent. {pp} For the next sixteen years, Poland barely closed the gap. In 2008, Slovenia was still about sixty percent richer. {p} Then the line falls off a cliff.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Slovenia (annual %); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Slovenia's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} In 2007, it grew seven percent. {pp} Then the 2008 crisis. In 2009, it shrank seven point six percent. Poland grew two point six. {p} And it didn't bounce back: Slovenia shrank again in 2012, and again in 2013. {pp} In December 2013, the government put about three billion euros into its banks, and avoided an international bailout.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH, compounded), population (LP)
shots.title: The crash
shots.narration: Put it together. From 2008 to 2013, after inflation, Slovenia's economy shrank about nine percent. Poland's grew about fourteen. {p} And over thirty years, from 1995 to 2025, Slovenia's economy roughly doubled. Poland's roughly tripled. {pp} Slovenia has about two million people. Poland has seventeen times as many.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: But here's the twist. In plain dollars, at market exchange rates, the picture is very different. {p} This year, Slovenia is about forty-one thousand six hundred dollars a person. Poland, about thirty-one thousand two hundred. {pp} That's still a third more. {p} Prices in Slovenia are higher, so adjusting for prices shrinks the gap. In plain money, Slovenia is still clearly ahead.
And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. {p} Now, the bigger race.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Slovenia, Czechia, Hungary and Poland. {p} In 2004, adjusted for prices, Slovenia was first and Poland was last. {pp} Since then, Czechia has passed Slovenia. Poland has passed Hungary. {p} And in the IMF's forecast, Poland ends up right on Slovenia's heels.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.title: The almost-pass, adjusted for prices
shots.narration: So here's where it stands, in the IMF's numbers. {p} In 2008, Slovenia was ahead by about twelve thousand dollars per person. {p} This year, about two thousand two hundred. {pp} And in 2031, in the IMF's forecast, about four hundred dollars. {p} That's half a percent. Not a pass, but close enough to call it a tie.

<soft>So, what's your guess?</soft> {pp} Does Poland pass Slovenia before 2031, {p} after, {p} or never? {pp} Tell me in the comments. {pp} If you're watching from Slovenia: {p} does it feel like this where you are? {pp} I read every comment.
And if you missed it, {p} this is the one where Hungary was twenty-nine percent richer, and Poland passed. {pp} It's right here. {pp} I'm Chartbound. {p} See you in the next one.

checks.say: 2004: SVN > CZE > HUN > POL (richer than Czechia, Hungary, Poland)
USD 2026: SVN ≈ 41,600, POL ≈ 31,200; ratio ≈ 1.33 (a third more)
2026: CZE > SVN (Czechia passed), POL > HUN; 2004: SVN > CZE

yt.title: Slovenia Was 71% Richer Than Poland. Now It's Almost Even.
yt.description:
Income per person adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): in 1995 the average Slovenian was 71% ahead of the average Pole. This year the gap is under 4%, and in the IMF's 2031 forecast it's about half a percent. The 2009 crash (−7.6%), the second recession in 2012–2013, the €3 billion bank rescue of December 2013, why Slovenia is still a third richer in plain dollars, and the race with Czechia and Hungary.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP); Bank of Slovenia, stress test results (December 2013). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
